---
title: "Session 0: You have been sent eDNA data. What do you do?"

---

```{r chunk-options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = TRUE,
  error = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

```{r table-helper, include=FALSE}
preview_table <- function(x, caption, n = 6) {
  knitr::kable(
    head(x, n),
    format = "html",
    caption = caption,
    digits = 2,
    row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = gsub("_", " ", names(x)),
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-condensed"'
  )
}
```

## We show you in this tutorial

In this session, we will go through the checks and steps you must do to have a working and interpretable dataset. 

We will achieve this by:

1. Join read data to their assigned taxonomic units. 
2. Check laboratory controls for potential sources of contamination. 
3. Apply filters to remove contamination, and other weak-signal data. 
4. Prepare community matrices alongside the associated metadata. 
5. Explore sequencing depth and species accumulation over effort.

Here, we will use the example of an 18S dataset targeting metazoan invertebrates in a Scottish landscape and across four habitat types, heath, regen, commercial woodland, and mature woodland. 



## 1. Prepare the working environment

To work with this code, you may either copy the code chunks directly to your own script, or download the .Rmd files associated to this repository. You can return to the repository with the link on the top right of the navigation bar.  

First, we need to prepare our environment, by installing the packages that contain the functions that we will use. It only needs doing once. 

```{r install-packages, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(
  c("here", "tidyverse", "janitor", "vegan", "iNEXT")
)
```

After installing, we load them into the session, this needs doing every time we open R. You may need to adjust file paths to the source of your files, if you are not working out of a cloned repository. 

```{r packages}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(vegan)
library(iNEXT)

# Declare this document's location relative to the project root.
here::i_am("session0.Rmd")

```

### Analysis settings

We declare a few values in advance, as it makes it easier to explore how different filtering decisions affect the results. These include the confidence thresholds for taxonomic assignments and other relevant values. 

The values below reproduce the thresholds in the original workflow.
They are choices for this dataset rather than universal defaults.

```{r analysis-settings}
tax_ranks <- c(
  "species", "genus", "family", "order",
  "class", "phylum", "kingdom"
)

habitat_levels <- c(
  "heath", "regen", "com_wood", "mat_wood"
)

confidence_cutoff <- 0.7
relative_cutoff <- 0.001
min_reads <- 3000

positive_control_taxon <- "Mesembrina_mystacea"


data_dir <- here::here("data", "session0")
```

A 70% confidence cutoff is the recommendation by the designers of the taxonomic classifier, called [RDP naïve Bayesian classifier](https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.00062-07). A 0.1% filter is also typically used in eDNA studies to dismiss nuisance detections and focus on ecologically relevant data. A few samples were further removed if they did not have at least 3,000 reads, supported by rarefaction analysis. 


## 2. Read the four input tables

Now we load our data. This will be acombination of data you hold, such as environmental metadata, and data that is sent to you. The latter, are typically in a "text" format, and split in several ways. Here, we have an ASV_table, which has ASV IDs as rows, and the lab IDs of samples as columns. The values within the cells correspond to the number of reads for a given ASV in a given sample. We also have the ASV_tax. This one has the taxonomic assignment for each ASV. We then have a conversion table from lab ID to field ID for our samples. Lastly, the metadata. The four are connected through identifiers, and can be merged as follows:

- `asv_id` connects read counts to taxonomy.
- `lab_id` connects sequencing columns to laboratory records and metadata.
- `sample_id` identifies the biological samples used in the analyses.

We are creating a "list" of our data files that call in later. File paths are the culprit for most issues at this stage.

```{r locate-inputs}
input_files <- c(
  counts = file.path(data_dir, "ASV_table.tsv"),
  taxonomy = file.path(data_dir, "ASV_tax_session0.csv"),
  lab_lookup = file.path(data_dir, "lab_field_id.csv"),
  metadata = file.path(data_dir, "CC_metadata_session0.csv")
)

```


### ASV counts

The count table is initially wide: each laboratory sample occupies a
separate column.Typically, we want to work with a long format, where sample_id is one column, we will address this later. 

```{r read-counts}
asv_tab <- read_tsv(
  input_files[["counts"]],
  show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(asv_id = str_trim(asv_id))


preview_table(
  asv_tab %>% select(1:6),
  "ASV read counts: first six rows and columns")
  
```


### Taxonomic assignments

This file contains the prepared rank hierarchy and assignment confidence
for each ASV. The taxonomic harmonisation that produced it is an upstream
preparation step.

```{r read-taxonomy}
asv_tax <- read_csv(
  input_files[["taxonomy"]],
  show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(asv_id = str_trim(asv_id))

preview_table(
  asv_tax %>%
    select(asv_id, kingdom, phylum, confidence),
  "Taxonomic assignments: first six records"
)

```

In these calls to the data, we are explicitly declaring the types of data of various columns. This can help avoid certain issues, but for most datasets, is not needed. 

### Laboratory-to-field lookup

The lookup connects laboratory identifiers to field records. We need to do some cleaning up here to make sure things match later. 

```{r read-laboratory-lookup}
lab_field_id <- read_csv(
  input_files[["lab_lookup"]],
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(field_id_lab = field_id) %>%
  mutate(
    lab_id = str_to_upper(str_trim(lab_id)),
    field_id_lab = na_if(str_trim(field_id_lab), ""),
    .keep = "none"
  )

preview_table(
  lab_field_id %>%
    select(lab_id, field_id_lab),
  "Lab to field lookup: first six records"
)
```

### Sample metadata

Even though we will drop some of the samples on the eDNA side, because of low read depth, we keep metadata complete to keep track of things.

```{r read-metadata}
metadata_cc <- read_csv(
  input_files[["metadata"]],
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    sample_id = str_trim(sample_id),
    lab_id = na_if(str_to_upper(str_trim(lab_id)), ""),
    treatment = factor(
      str_trim(treatment),
      levels = habitat_levels
    )
  )
metadata_lab <- metadata_cc %>%
  filter(!is.na(lab_id))

preview_table(
  metadata_cc %>%
    select(sample_id, site_id, treatment, ph, moisture, temp),
  "Sample metadata: selected measurements for the first six records"
)
```

We have measured several bits of information. For each site, of which there are 20, we have three plots. Each plot is identified by their distance 00m, 05m, and 15m. These are meters along a transect. At each plot, we collect one sample, which is a composite of three cores. We also collect pH, soil temperature, and moisture. For each site, we also collect vegetation data at a 5-meter by 5-meter quadrat. 


## 3. A Few Things to Consider

### Mixed Taxonomy

An ASV may have a species assignment, a genus assignment, or only a higher-rank assignment. Here, we use something called mixed taxonomy. Rather than dropping higher level assignments, we treat them as if they represented at least one other taxa. 


```{r taxonomic-labels}
asv_tax <- asv_tax %>%
  mutate(
    consensus_name = coalesce(
      species, genus, family, order,
      class, phylum, kingdom
    )
  )
```

This is why we typically refer to taxa, rather than species. 


### Fixing Mistakes

Mistakes are unavoidable. Here, the positive and negative control and a sample got mixed up in the 96-well plate. This was obvious when exploring the controls (below): 

- `PC03` becomes `AP845`.
- `NC03` becomes `PC03`.

To do this, we take the lab names from the asv_table, and rename them to the right ID. 

```{r sample-key}
sample_key <- tibble(
  lab_id_original = setdiff(names(asv_tab), "asv_id")
) %>%
  mutate(lab_id = str_to_upper(lab_id_original))


  sample_key <- sample_key %>%
    mutate(
      lab_id = case_when(
        lab_id == "PC03" ~ "AP845",
        lab_id == "NC03" ~ "PC03",
        TRUE ~ lab_id
      ) )

```

Now that we have the right IDs, we can use the same table, to separate a few things. Currently we have two types of samples. True samples, and controls. Controls include extraction controls, positive controls, and negative controls. 
- Extraction controls are tubes where no sample is added, but where the same process and ragents are added as if DNA was being extracted. They are used to monitor contamination during the DNA extraction.
- Positive controls are used at the library preparation stage, and have all the reagents plus a known source of DNA. Here we have used the DNA of a fly. It monitors whether lab stages are working correctly. 
- Negative controls are also used during library preparation. Like DNA extractions, they receive all the reagents, but no DNA. It monitors contamination during library preparation. 

```{r classify-samples}
sample_key <- sample_key %>%
  # Attach field labels to distinguish extraction controls.
  left_join(
    lab_field_id,
    by = "lab_id"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    sample_type = case_when(
      str_detect(lab_id, "^PC") ~ "PCR positive",
      str_detect(lab_id, "^NC") ~ "PCR negative",
      str_detect(
        coalesce(field_id_lab, ""),
        regex("extraction|blank", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "Extraction blank",
      TRUE ~ "Field sample"
    )
  )


sample_key %>%
  count(sample_type, name = "n_laboratory_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

None of the negative controls had any DNA, all six positive controls returned DNA, and only two out of seven extractions controls had any DNA detected. 



## 4. Giving the data the right "shape"

As mentioned earlier, the ASV_table is in a wide format, and for now, we prefer to work with a long format. That means that all the ASVs within a sample, get a row. A long format is easier to handle when trying to apply filters across samples, and explore the data visually. 

We will get rid of rows where ASVs have zero reads in a given sample, to keep the table to a reasonable size. They will come back later. 

```{r long-detection-table}
asv_long <- asv_tab %>%
  # Turn the laboratory-sample columns into identifier–count pairs.
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -asv_id,
    names_to = "lab_id_original",
    values_to = "reads"
  ) %>%
  filter(reads > 0) %>%

  # Attach corrected laboratory IDs and sample classifications.
  left_join(
    sample_key,
    by = "lab_id_original"
  ) %>%

  # Attach one prepared taxonomy record to each ASV.
  left_join(
    asv_tax,
    by = "asv_id"
  )

preview_table(
  asv_long %>% select(1:10) %>% arrange(lab_id_original),
  "ASV read counts: first six rows and columns") 
```



## 5. Inspect the Contamination and Controls

We keep all rows that belong to a non-field sample, and visualise them below. 

```{r aggregate-controls}
controls <- asv_long %>%
  filter(
    sample_type != "Field sample") %>%
  group_by(
    lab_id, sample_type, consensus_name,
    across(all_of(tax_ranks))
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    reads = sum(reads),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

### Visualise control detections

Here we create a tile heatmap that shows us if there are problematic controls. 

```{r control-heatmap, fig.height=7}

  control_counts <- controls %>%
    group_by(lab_id, sample_type, consensus_name) %>%
    summarise(reads = sum(reads), .groups = "drop")


  ggplot(
    control_counts,
    aes(
      x = lab_id,
      y = fct_rev(factor(consensus_name)),
      fill = reads
    )
  ) +
    geom_tile(colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
      name = "Read counts",
      colours = c("white", "red", "black"),
      values = c(0, 0.1, 1),
      limits = c(0, NA)
    ) +
    facet_grid(
      . ~ sample_type,
      scales = "free_x",
      space = "free_x"
    ) +
    labs(
      x = "Process controls",
      y = "Taxonomic assignment"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
      axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic")
    )


```
Here we see the two extraction blanks that yielded DNA. In AP818 it belong to *Oribatida*, in AP910 *Metaterotocephalus crassidens* a type of microscopic nematode. *Oribatida* are group of mites. *Mesembrina mystacea* is a positive control, and is found consistently across all six of them. Two positive controls also have insect DNA, which probably corresponds to unassigned DNA of the same fly. Because *M. crassidens* has several hundred reads, we will establish a threshold, such that for this species to be considered present in a sample, it has to have at least one more read count than it does in this extraction control. This contributes to reduce potential contaminant detections.  



### Contamination Thresholds

For each taxa detected in the controls, we take the largest count observed. This count will be subtracted from the corresponding field-sample count.


```{r control-thresholds}
control_thresholds <- controls %>%
  filter(consensus_name != positive_control_taxon) %>%
  group_by(across(all_of(tax_ranks))) %>%
  summarise(
    threshold = max(reads),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```


## 6. Cleaning the data

### Keeping taxonomic assignments with high confidence

Before we remove contaminants, we will remove detections that have low confidence (<70%). 


```{r select-field-detections}
field_detections <- asv_long %>%
  filter(
    sample_type == "Field sample",
    confidence >= confidence_cutoff
  ) 
```

### Combine ASVs with the same assignment

Multiple ASVs may be assigned to the same taxa. Including two ASVs in the same sample. So we combine those, before we apply contamination thresholds. 


```{r aggregate-field-counts}
field_counts <- field_detections %>%
  group_by(
    lab_id, consensus_name,
    across(all_of(tax_ranks))
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    reads = sum(reads),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Contamination thresholds

We combine the field_counts which has each sample's and taxa read data with the contamination threshold dataset we created earlier. We then do the difference, and detections that drop to zero, we remove.

```{r subtract-control-counts}
field_corrected <- field_counts %>%
  left_join(
    control_thresholds,
    by = tax_ranks) %>%
  mutate(
    threshold = replace_na(threshold, 0),

    # Clamp corrected counts at zero before removing non-detections.
    reads = pmax(reads - threshold, 0)
  ) %>%
  filter(reads > 0)
```

### Final filter

eDNA is a "noisy" business, and typically, thresholds of relative frequency of reads are used to prevent the data from being swamped by many low read taxa. We use a 0.1% relative read frequency threshold. 

```{r relative-frequency-filter}
asv_clean <- field_corrected %>%
  group_by(lab_id) %>%
  mutate(relfreq = reads / sum(reads)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(relfreq > relative_cutoff) %>%

  # Recalculate totals after the low-frequency detections are removed.
  group_by(lab_id) %>%
  mutate(
    total_reads = sum(reads),
    relfreq = reads / total_reads
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```



## 7. Attach Environmental  Metadata

Attach the study metadata using the laboratory identifier.

```{r attach-metadata}
asv_cc <- asv_clean %>%
  left_join(
    metadata_lab,
    by = "lab_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(sample_id))

```

### Have we lost any samples?

We use the metadata table as the full record of samples.


```{r first-retention-audit}
sample_audit <- metadata_cc %>%
  mutate(
    in_count_table = lab_id %in% sample_key$lab_id,
    has_filtered_detections = sample_id %in% asv_cc$sample_id,

    status_before_depth = case_when(
      !in_count_table ~ "Absent from count table",
      !has_filtered_detections ~ "No detections after filtering",
      TRUE ~ "Retained before depth filter"
    )
  )

sample_audit %>%
  count(treatment, status_before_depth, name = "n_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

No samples lost at this stage. 


## 8. Community Matrix - back to wide

We took wide datasets, and made them long. However, many of the tools for analysis we will use later on, want wide datasets. This is typical of multivariate analysis methods like NMDS, or RDA. They take a community matrix as the basic input, and then separate matrices for other inputs like environmental metadata. 

While our original ASV_table was ASV (rows) by Samples (columns), community matrices are Samples (rows) by Taxa (columns).  

This will bring back the zeroes we discarded earlier too. You will want to save this as an output for later analyses. 


```{r community-matrix}
comm <- asv_cc %>%
  select(sample_id, consensus_name, reads) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = consensus_name,
    values_from = reads,
    values_fill = 0,
    values_fn = sum
  ) %>%
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") %>%
  as.matrix()

```

### Reading Depth

Once you have a working dataset, you might want to extract some information. A typical metric is average reading depth and the range. This is the number of sequence read that have survived in each sample. 


```{r filtered-read-depth}
read_depth <- asv_cc %>%
  distinct(sample_id, treatment, total_reads)

read_depth %>%
  summarise(
    mean_reads = mean(total_reads),
    min_reads = min(total_reads),
    max_reads = max(total_reads)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

We are in the realm of 10k reads, whether this is sufficient or not depends on your target species and their inherent diversity per sample. For researchers working with viruses, typically they need millions of reads, for researchers studying predator diets where each sample may have less than 10 species, thousands are typically enough. Here, we are in an intermediate space, but we can evaluate whether it is enough or not. 

## 9. Explore read-based rarefaction

Rarefaction curves lets us evaluate whether the "sampling effort", in our case, reading depth, is enough to capture the diversity within a sample. It is strikingly simple, but equally useful. For each sample, we will sample one read at a time (or groups of 10 or 100 reads), and we will look at how many taxa  we recover. We will do that repeatedly until we run out of reads to take from the samples, and each time, we look at the taxa we recover. If we find new taxa, we add them to the previous figure of taxa. If we have enough "effort", should run out of new taxa before we run out of reads. If we plot this, we should see a line that plateaus.  


```{r calculate-rarefaction}
rarecurve_df <- vegan::rarecurve(
  comm,
  step = 100,
  label = FALSE,
  tidy = TRUE
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(sample_id = as.character(Site)) %>%

  # Attach habitat information to each sample's curve.
  left_join(
    metadata_cc %>% select(sample_id, treatment),
    by = "sample_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )
```
First we calculate it. Now we plot it. 

The vertical line marks the proposed minimum filtered read depth.

```{r plot-rarefaction}
p_rare <- ggplot(
  rarecurve_df,
  aes(x = Sample, y = Species, group = sample_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = min_reads,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    x = "Filtered sequencing depth (reads)",
    y = "Expected retained taxonomic labels"
  )

p_rare
```
We have drawn a vertical dashed line at 3,000 reads, based on an earlier exploration of the data. We can see that after this point ,all lines flatten. 

We can zoom in further. 

```{r zoom-rarefaction, eval=FALSE}
p_rare + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5000))
```
Some of the lines to the left of 3,000 are not yet flat. The issue with these samples is that we have "missed" taxa in them, and thus they may skew our metrics of richness. 

At this point we have a choice. Increasing read depth typically leads to increased taxonomic richness. To address this, we can rarefy our data, this means that we only keep as many reads as there are in our sample with the fewest reads. The problem with doing this, is that if your lowest is *too* low, you might lose valuable information from your other samples. Alternatively, if most samples have flat curves, and only a few samples do not, it may be preferable to remove those samples. At that point, rarefying is not as important. Here, we have worked with relative read abundance instead of rarefied reads. Both arrive at a similar destination.  


## 10. Apply the minimum read-depth rule

As per our exploration we drop samples with fewer than 3,000 reads. 

```{r depth-retention-summary}
read_depth %>%
  mutate(retained = total_reads >= min_reads) %>%
  count(treatment, retained, name = "n_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```
We lose a total of seven samples out of 60. We revisit our community matrix. 

```{r retain-community-samples}
asv_final <- asv_cc %>%
  filter(total_reads >= min_reads)

comm_keep <- comm[
  rownames(comm) %in% asv_final$sample_id,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Remove taxonomic labels with no detections in the retained samples.
comm_keep <- comm_keep[
  ,
  colSums(comm_keep) > 0,
  drop = FALSE
]
```




### Match the metadata to the matrix

Because, we have removed data from the community matrix, we need to match this with our metadata table. 

we also want them to have the same order, so that they match in the internal machinery of our models. 

```{r align-metadata}
metadata_keep <- metadata_cc %>%
  slice(match(rownames(comm_keep), sample_id))

identical(rownames(comm_keep), metadata_keep$sample_id)

taxon_lookup <- asv_tax %>%
  filter(consensus_name %in% colnames(comm_keep)) %>%
  select(consensus_name, all_of(tax_ranks)) %>%
  distinct()

```


## 11. Final Matrices

Because of the issues around using read counts (or relative read counts), we might want to keep a presence-absence community matrix, and a relfreq matrix. 


```{r alternative-community-matrices}
comm_pa <- vegan::decostand(
  comm_keep,
  method = "pa"
)

comm_relfreq <- vegan::decostand(
  comm_keep,
  method = "total"
)


```



## 12. Species Accummulation Curves

In a similar way have assesed whether read depth was sufficient to capture sample-level richness. We can assess whether the sample size was enough to capture habitat-level richness. These are called species accummulation curve, and use the same process as described above, only at sample.

Here, we will use a package called iNEXT, which provides a more robust workflow by using permutation to provide confidence intervals. We must provide two things:

1. The total number of retained soil samples at a given habitat.
2. The number of those samples in which each taxonomic label was detected.

This format of data is called incidence-frequencies which we can prepare from the presence-absence community matrix.

```{r prepare-incidence-frequencies}
samples_by_habitat <- split(
  metadata_keep$sample_id,
  metadata_keep$treatment,
  drop = TRUE
)

inext_input <- purrr::map(
  samples_by_habitat,
  function(sample_ids) {

    mat <- comm_pa[sample_ids, , drop = FALSE]

    # Count detections across samples for each taxonomic label.
    freq <- colSums(mat)
    freq <- freq[freq > 0]

    # iNEXT requires the sampling-unit count as the first entry.
    c(nrow(mat), freq)
  }
)


```

### Estimate richness accumulation

iNEXT can provide a number of richness indicators, which we can select by changing the parameter q. Here we use `q = 0` for taxon richness. 

```{r estimate-accumulation}
set.seed(123) # keeps results reproduceable between runs. 

inext_results <- iNEXT::iNEXT(
  inext_input,
  q = 0,
  datatype = "incidence_freq",
  nboot = 100
)
```
After running this we can plot the curves. 

```{r plot-accumulation}
iNEXT::ggiNEXT(inext_results, type = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of soil samples",
    y = "Taxonomic-label richness",
    colour = "Habitat",
    fill = "Habitat"
  )
```
Here, our curves are far from flat suggesting that a substantial component of biodiversity has not been captures within each habitat at the current sample size of up to 15 samples per habitat. 

Due to the mathematical properties of a curve like this, which increases asymptotically towards the maximum taxon richess, we can extrapolate a predicted value for these maxima. 


### Percentage of richness captured

The asymptotic estimates concern the retained taxonomic labels under the
sampling and detection process represented by these data.

```{r richness-estimates}
inext_results$AsyEst %>%
  filter(Diversity == "Species richness") %>%
  select(
    Assemblage, Observed, Estimator, LCL, UCL
  ) %>%
  mutate(percentage = round((Observed/Estimator)*100,2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

We have captures between 57% and 75% of the predicted total richness across habitats. Note that the experimental design was not intended for a complete biodiversity inventory as much as a test of differences between habitat states. 


## 13. Save the prepared data for the next session

Save a dedicated Session 0 bundle rather than overwriting the original
multi-dataset RDS files.

The bundle contains the community matrices, aligned metadata, retained
taxonomy, sample audit, and filtering settings.

## 13. Export the prepared datasets

Now we have a better grasp of our dataset, and are able to use them in downstream analysis. 

We will export the various outputs. 

```{r export-session0-data}
derived_dir <- here::here("data", "derived")

dir.create(
  derived_dir,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# Retained read counts.
readr::write_csv(
  tibble::as_tibble(comm_keep, rownames = "sample_id"),
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa_counts.csv")
)

# Presence–absence.
readr::write_csv(
  tibble::as_tibble(comm_pa, rownames = "sample_id"),
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa_presence_absence.csv")
)

# Relative read frequencies.
readr::write_csv(
  tibble::as_tibble(comm_relfreq, rownames = "sample_id"),
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa_relative_frequencies.csv")
)

# Metadata for retained samples.
readr::write_csv(
  metadata_keep,
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa_metadata.csv")
)

# Retained taxonomic information.
readr::write_csv(
  taxon_lookup,
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa_taxonomy.csv")
)

# Record of sample retention and exclusion.
readr::write_csv(
  sample_audit,
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa_sample_audit.csv")
)
```

Session 1 will recover these datasets for this work.
